units.title: Bayesian tests still mislead when stopped on peeking thresholds

claim.text: The source states Bayesian A/B testing is not immune to peeking, reporting a simulation with about an 80% false positive rate when peeking every 100 observations and stopping at P(A>B)>0.95.
claim.quote: simulation showing about 80% false positive rate when peeking every 100 obs and stopping at P(A>B)>0.95

args.text: Peeking every 100 observations and stopping when P(A>B)>0.95.
args.quote: peeking every 100 obs and stopping at P(A>B)>0.95

unknowns: Simulation parameters (prior, effect size, other thresholds) are not given in the passage.
Not stated whether the ~80% figure generalises to other peek intervals or stopping thresholds.

units.title: CUPED is default-on in vendor tooling with a 30-50% sample-reduction claim

claim.text: The Optimizely and Datadog CUPED documentation is characterised as vendor implementation detail carrying a 30-50% sample reduction claim and default-on behaviour.
claim.quote: vendor implementation detail, 30-50% sample reduction claim, default-on behaviour

unknowns: The 30-50% sample reduction is an attributed vendor claim, not independently verified in the passage.
Which metrics, traffic levels or effect sizes the reduction applies to is not stated.

units.title: Prioritize tests with the PXL scorecard

claim.text: PXL is described as a binary, evidence-weighted scorecard and an antidote to subjective ICE prioritization.
claim.quote: the actual PXL binary/evidence-weighted scorecard, an antidote to subjective ICE

action.text: Use the PXL binary, evidence-weighted scorecard to prioritize A/B tests instead of subjective ICE scoring.
action.quote: the actual PXL binary/evidence-weighted scorecard, an antidote to subjective ICE

unknowns: The PXL scoring criteria and weights themselves are not provided in the passage.
The source is Tier 3 (named practitioner).

units.title: Named conditions for running bandit tests

claim.text: The source names short campaigns, headlines and promotions as conditions for bandit tests, alongside Stephen Pavlovich's ecommerce reasoning on regret.
claim.quote: named conditions (short campaigns, headlines, promotions) with Stephen Pavlovich's ecommerce reasoning on regret

unknowns: Whether the listed conditions are individually sufficient or jointly required is not stated.
The regret reasoning itself is not reproduced in the passage.

units.title: 100 conversions per variant is not a stopping threshold

claim.text: The source debunks magic conversion-number rules and shows why 100 conversions per variant is not a threshold.
claim.quote: shows why 100/variant is not a threshold

unknowns: The correct stopping criterion is not stated in the passage.
Source of the debunking argument is not reproduced in the passage.

units.title: Detect sample ratio mismatch with the chi-square method

claim.text: Sample ratio mismatch work is described as using the chi-square method with a worked p-value example and a ~6% Microsoft rate.
claim.quote: chi-square method, worked p-value example, ~6% Microsoft rate

action.text: Use the chi-square method with a worked p-value example to detect sample ratio mismatch.

unknowns: The significance threshold used for the chi-square test is not stated in the passage.
Whether ~6% is per experiment or uses another denominator is not stated.

units.title: Baymard checkout benchmarks as evidence for big-swing hypotheses

claim.text: Baymard reports 70.22% global average cart abandonment from a meta-analysis of 50 studies (last updated September 22 2025; the rate has held 69-71% since 2014), 11.3 average checkout form fields, up to 35.26% achievable checkout uplift, and about $260B recoverable orders across US/EU.
claim.quote: 70.22% global average cart abandonment from a meta-analysis of 50 studies

unknowns: Composition of the 50 studies and the baseline behind the 35.26% uplift figure are not given.
Denominators behind the $260B recoverable-orders estimate are not stated.

units.title: Shopify checkout testability is plan-dependent and client-side testing was killed in August 2024

claim.text: What is testable on Shopify is described as plan-dependent, and an August 2024 extensibility change is said to have killed client-side checkout A/B testing.
claim.quote: the August 2024 extensibility change that killed client-side checkout A/B testing

unknowns: Which Shopify plan permits which test types is not detailed in the passage.
The exact mechanics of the August 2024 extensibility change are not described.

units.title: No built-in Shopify checkout-extensibility A/B rule

claim.text: Shopify community confirmation is cited that there is no built-in checkout-extensibility A/B rule to show or hide customisations per group.
claim.quote: official confirmation there is no built-in checkout-extensibility A/B rule to show/hide customisations per group

unknowns: Whether any workaround exists is not stated in the passage.
Whether the confirmation still holds is not established from a current primary source in the passage.

units.title: Company-by-company win-rate and false-positive-risk table

claim.text: A company-by-company win-rate and false-positive-risk table with citations reports Microsoft 33%, Bing 15%, Booking/Google/Netflix 10% and Airbnb 8%.
claim.quote: the company-by-company win-rate and false-positive-risk table (Microsoft 33%, Bing 15%, Booking/Google/Netflix 10%, Airbnb 8%) with citations

unknowns: Definitions of win rate and false-positive risk, plus underlying test counts, are not in the passage.
The table is a second-hand report of Kohavi data (Tier 2).

units.title: Named-sample ecommerce win rates from a test database

claim.text: A real test database is reported to give named-sample ecommerce win rates of 36.3% win, 41.6% inconclusive and +2.77% median RPV, with the caveat that research pre-qualification raises win rate.
claim.quote: named-sample ecommerce win rates (36.3% win, 41.6% inconclusive, +2.77% median RPV) from a real test database

unknowns: Sample size and time period of the database are not given.
The denominator behind median RPV is not stated.
Tier 3 source.

units.title: Winsorize high-variance revenue metrics

claim.text: Concrete variance figures are reported for revenue metrics (97% spend $0, CoV ~750%, revenue needs ~6x traffic, 28k vs 175k per variant) together with a winsorization workaround.
claim.quote: the concrete variance numbers (97% spend $0, CoV ~750%, revenue needs ~6x traffic, 28k vs 175k per variant) and the winsorization workaround

action.text: Apply winsorization as a workaround for high-variance revenue metrics.

unknowns: Winsorization cut-offs or percentiles are not stated in the passage.
Figures are attributed to a Tier 3 blog (Atticus Li), March 2026.

units.title: CUPED has a ceiling on volatile revenue metrics

claim.text: A hard number is cited showing CUPED's Ceiling on volatile revenue metrics at 15.91% variance reduction on n=400,000, described as key evidence for why CUPED underdelivers on DTC revenue.
claim.quote: the hard number showing CUPED's ceiling on volatile revenue metrics (15.91% variance reduction on n=400,000)

unknowns: The metric definition and experiment context for the 15.91% figure are not in the passage.
Whether the ceiling transfers to DTC revenue settings is asserted, not demonstrated, in the passage.

units.title: Anti-flicker page hiding costs 3-4 seconds

claim.text: The sources cover the FOOC mechanism, state there is no miracle fix, and report a 3-4s anti-flicker page-hide cost (DebugBear, Feb 2022, updated Dec 2025).
claim.quote: and the 3-4s anti-flicker page-hide cost (DebugBear, Feb 2022, updated Dec 2025)

unknowns: The measurement method behind the 3-4s cost is not stated in the passage.
No alternative anti-flicker approach is given beyond the absence of a miracle fix.

units.title: Bold changes only under 100,000 visitors per month, with holdout re-testing

claim.text: The source sets an under-100,000-visitors-per-month bold-changes-only gate and a re-test-surprising-winners-with-a-holdout rule.
claim.quote: the under-100,000-visitors/month "bold changes only" gate and re-test-surprising-winners-with-a-holdout rule

action.text: Below 100,000 visitors per month, test only bold changes and re-test surprising winners with a holdout.
action.quote: the under-100,000-visitors/month "bold changes only" gate and re-test-surprising-winners-with-a-holdout rule

unknowns: Whether the 100,000-visitors/month gate is site-wide or page-level is not stated.
This is a Tier 3 heuristic; its derivation is not given in the passage.
Holdout duration and size are not stated.

units.title: Test price framing rather than the price number

claim.text: For pricing tests the source cites the Amazon 2000 case (6,896 refunds, $3.10 average), an EU personalised-price disclosure rule, negative vs positive price discrimination, and advises testing framing rather than the number.

action.text: Test the framing of a price rather than the price number itself.

unknowns: The Amazon case details and the jurisdiction(s) where the EU disclosure rule applies are not elaborated in the passage.
Whether the EU disclosure rule is a legal prerequisite for personalised-price tests is not stated explicitly.
Tier 3 sources.

Unresolved values: reported win rates differ across sources (36.3% for the DRIP database, 19.1% for the 2,288-test ConversionTeam sample, 10% for the Thomke/Ghosh Optimizely meta-analysis, 8-33% in the company table). The passage does not reconcile them; they carry different samples, definitions and thresholds, and some are Tier 3.

Unresolved platform behaviour: the passage asserts that an August 2024 Shopify change killed client-side checkout A/B testing and that no built-in checkout-extensibility A/B rule exists. Any live deployment depending on this needs current primary-source verification; the passage does not supply the current platform documentation.

Unresolved spans: the 30-50% CUPED sample reduction (u2), the 15.91% variance reduction on n=400,000 (u13), the ~6% Microsoft SRM rate (u6) and the 3-4s anti-flicker page-hide cost (u14) lack stated denominators, measurement methods or experiment context within the passage.

source.text:
Bayesian A/B Testing Is Not Immune to Peeking. Alex Molas. alexmolas.com, October 30 2025. https://www.alexmolas.com/2025/10/30/bayesian-ab-test-peeking.html Tier 2. Topics: 3,5. Why: simulation showing about 80% false positive rate when peeking every 100 obs and stopping at P(A>B)>0.95; corrects a common Bayesian myth.

CUPED variance reduction docs. Optimizely and Datadog. https://support.optimizely.com/hc/en-us/articles/33424529987597 and https://docs.datadoghq.com/experiments/statistics/cuped/ Tier 1. Topics: 7. Why: vendor implementation detail, 30-50% sample reduction claim, default-on behaviour.

PXL: A Better Way to Prioritize Your A/B Tests. Peep Laja / CXL. https://cxl.com/blog/better-way-prioritize-ab-tests/ Tier 3 (named practitioner). Topics: 9. Why: the actual PXL binary/evidence-weighted scorecard, an antidote to subjective ICE.

Guide to Multi-Armed Bandit: When to Do Bandit Tests. CXL. https://cxl.com/blog/bandit-tests/ Tier 3. Topics: 8. Why: named conditions (short campaigns, headlines, promotions) with Stephen Pavlovich's ecommerce reasoning on regret.

Stopping A/B Tests: How Many Conversions Do I Need? CXL. https://cxl.com/blog/stopping-ab-tests-how-many-conversions-do-i-need/ Tier 3. Topics: 1,2,4,13. Why: debunks "magic conversion number" rules and shows why 100/variant is not a threshold.

Sample ratio mismatch. Wikipedia + Automated SRM Detection (Gupta, Kohavi et al., ACM 2022). https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sample_ratio_mismatch and https://dl.acm.org/doi/fullHtml/10.1145/3530019.3534982 Tier 1/2. Topics: 6. Why: chi-square method, worked p-value example, ~6% Microsoft rate.

Cart & Checkout UX research. Baymard Institute. https://baymard.com/blog/collections/cart-and-checkout Tier 1/2. Topics: 4,9,12. Why: 70.22% global average cart abandonment from a meta-analysis of 50 studies (last updated September 22 2025; the rate has held 69-71% since 2014), 11.3 average checkout form fields, up to 35.26% achievable checkout uplift and about $260B recoverable orders across US/EU; evidence for big-swing checkout hypotheses.

A/B Testing on Shopify without Plus / Shopify Plus checkout extensibility. Varify.io and Convert.com. https://varify.io/en/shopify-ab-testing-without-plus/ and https://www.convert.com/blog/shopify-ab-testing/optimize-shopify-checkout/ Tier 1/3. Topics: 12. Why: what is testable per Shopify plan, and the August 2024 extensibility change that killed client-side checkout A/B testing.

A/B testing on Shopify Checkout page. Shopify Developer Community (Liam-Shopify). shopify.dev, Nov-Dec 2024. https://community.shopify.dev/t/a-b-testing-on-shopify-checkout-page/3246 Tier 1. Considered and rejected

Generic "A/B testing statistics" listicles quoting round win-rate numbers with no sample (multiple). Rejected: violate the no-sample-size rule; win rates cited without the test count or confidence threshold.

Vendor case studies claiming large lifts (e.g. "+364%") without stating sample, duration, and baseline. Rejected under Twyman's law; these are the single most common source of bad knowledge in this field. Keep only as unvalidated hypothesis material.

abtestpro.com and similar auto-generated calculator/learn pages. Rejected as primary: they restate Evan Miller correctly but add no independent evidence; cite Miller directly instead.

HubSpot "20,000 rule" post. Partially used for the claim-2 check only; rejected as a general source because it is email-list-oriented and the round-number rule does not generalise across baselines.

LinkedIn and Medium opinion posts without data. Rejected as Tier 4 except where they present a named simulation (Molas) or concrete platform numbers (Atticus Li).

Notes on confidence and conflicts

The sample-size tables from calculator sites agree with each other and with Evan Miller's n=16 formula to within rounding. Treat them as reliable. Small differences between calculators come from the leading constant (Miller uses a value slightly below 16) and from pooled vs unpooled variance.
